questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
points: Brief intro: who you are, current year/degree, core interest area
1-2 highlights (a project, internship, or achievement)
Why you're a fit for the kind of role you're applying to
Keep it under 60-90 seconds when spoken aloud

questions.question: Why should we hire you?
points: Name specific skills that match the job requirement
Back each skill with a concrete example (project/internship)
Mention a soft skill (teamwork, ownership, learning speed)
Avoid generic claims with no evidence behind them

questions.question: Describe a challenging situation and how you handled it.
points: Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Focus on YOUR specific actions, not the team's in general
State a measurable or clear outcome
Pick a real, specific example — not a vague generality

questions.question: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
points: Strength: relevant to the role, with a quick example
Weakness: genuine, not a disguised humble-brag
Show what you're actively doing to improve the weakness
Keep both answers concise, not a long list

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
points: Show realistic ambition tied to the role/industry
Mention growth in skills or responsibility, not just a job title
Connect it back to why this company/role helps get there
Avoid answers that sound unrelated to the job you're applying for

questions.question: Why do you want to work at our company?
points: Reference something specific about the company (product, values, work)
Connect it to your own skills or interests
Avoid generic answers that could apply to any company
Shows you've actually researched them beforehand

questions.question: Describe a time you worked in a team and faced a conflict.
points: Briefly explain the disagreement without blaming anyone
Focus on how you communicated or resolved it
State what the team learned or how it improved outcomes
Shows maturity and collaboration, not just 'I was right'

questions.question: How do you handle pressure or tight deadlines?
points: Give a concrete example, not just a general statement
Mention a specific technique (prioritizing, breaking tasks down)
Show the outcome was still good despite the pressure
Avoid claiming you 'never' feel stressed — sound authentic

questions.question: Do you have any questions for us?
points: Always have at least 1-2 questions ready — never say 'no'
Ask about the team, tech stack, or growth opportunities
Avoid asking only about salary/perks at this stage
Shows genuine interest in the role beyond just getting hired

questions.question: Why did you choose this field/branch of study?
points: Give a genuine reason (interest, a project, an experience)
Connect it to what you enjoy doing day-to-day in this field
Keep it honest rather than an overly rehearsed line
Bonus: mention something you did beyond the syllabus

questions.question: What is the Virtual DOM and why does React use it?
points: Explain it's an in-memory representation of the real DOM
Mention diffing/reconciliation to find minimal changes
Why: direct DOM manipulation is slow, this batches updates
Bonus: mention keys and how they help the diffing algorithm

questions.question: Explain the difference between state and props in React.
points: Props: passed from parent, read-only in the child
State: managed internally within a component, can change
Changing state triggers a re-render, props don't own their data
Give a small example of each

questions.question: What is the CSS box model?
points: Content, padding, border, margin — in that order
Explain box-sizing: content-box vs border-box
Mention how it affects element sizing calculations
Bonus: give a practical bug this misunderstanding causes

questions.question: How does event delegation work in JavaScript?
points: Events bubble up from child to parent elements
Attach one listener to a parent instead of many on children
Mention e.target vs e.currentTarget
Why it's useful: performance, works for dynamically added elements

questions.question: What are React hooks and why were they introduced?
points: Functions that let you use state/lifecycle in function components
Name a few: useState, useEffect, useContext
Why: avoid class components, better logic reuse (custom hooks)
Mention rules of hooks (top-level, only in React functions)

questions.question: What is responsive web design and how do you implement it?
points: Design that adapts to different screen sizes/devices
Mention media queries, flexible grids, relative units (%, rem)
Mobile-first vs desktop-first approach
Bonus: mention flexbox/grid or a framework like Tailwind

questions.question: What is REST and what makes an API RESTful?
points: Representational State Transfer — architectural style, not a protocol
Stateless requests, resource-based URLs, standard HTTP methods
Mention proper status codes (200, 201, 404, 500)
Bonus: idempotency of GET/PUT vs POST

questions.question: Explain the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases.
points: SQL: structured schema, relational, ACID compliant
NoSQL: flexible schema, document/key-value/graph based
When to use which — structured relational data vs flexible/scaling needs
Give an example of each (MySQL vs MongoDB)

questions.question: What is middleware in a framework like Express.js?
points: Functions that run between the request and the final handler
Access to req, res, and next()
Common uses: auth checks, logging, parsing request bodies
Mention middleware order matters

questions.question: How do you handle authentication in a web application?
points: Explain session-based vs token-based (JWT) authentication
Mention password hashing (bcrypt) — never store plain text
Where the token is stored and sent (headers, cookies)
Bonus: mention refresh tokens or token expiry

questions.question: What is database indexing and why is it useful?
points: A data structure that speeds up lookups on a column
Trade-off: faster reads, slower writes, extra storage
When to use it: columns frequently searched/filtered/joined on
Bonus: mention a specific index type (B-tree)

questions.question: What are microservices and what problems do they solve?
points: Breaking an app into small, independently deployable services
Benefits: independent scaling, tech flexibility, fault isolation
Trade-offs: added complexity, network overhead, need for orchestration
Contrast briefly with a monolithic architecture

questions.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
points: Supervised: trained on labeled data (input-output pairs)
Unsupervised: finds patterns in unlabeled data
Give an example of each (classification vs clustering)
Bonus: mention semi-supervised or reinforcement learning exists too

questions.question: What is overfitting and how do you prevent it?
points: Model performs well on training data, poorly on unseen data
Prevention: more data, regularization, cross-validation
Mention simpler models or dropout (for neural nets)
Bonus: explain the bias-variance tradeoff briefly

questions.question: Explain the difference between precision and recall.
points: Precision: of predicted positives, how many were correct
Recall: of actual positives, how many were correctly identified
Mention there's a trade-off between the two
Give a real-world example where one matters more (e.g. medical screening)

questions.question: What is feature engineering and why does it matter?
points: Creating/transforming input variables to improve model performance
Examples: normalization, encoding categorical variables, new derived features
Why it matters: good features often matter more than the algorithm choice
Bonus: mention feature selection to reduce dimensionality

questions.question: What is the difference between a Type I and Type II error?
points: Type I: false positive — rejecting a true null hypothesis
Type II: false negative — failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Relate it back to precision/recall if helpful
Give a simple example (e.g. spam detection)

questions.question: How would you handle missing data in a dataset?
points: Mention checking why data is missing (random vs systematic)
Options: drop rows/columns, imputation (mean/median/mode), predictive imputation
Explain trade-offs of each approach
Bonus: mention flagging missingness itself as a feature

questions.question: What is the difference between a Machine Learning Engineer and a Data Scientist?
points: ML Engineer: focuses on deploying, scaling, productionizing models
Data Scientist: focuses more on analysis, experimentation, insights
Overlap exists but ML Engineers care more about pipelines/infra
Mention MLOps as a related concept

questions.question: What is gradient descent?
points: An optimization algorithm to minimize a loss function
Iteratively adjusts weights in the direction of steepest descent
Mention learning rate and its effect on convergence
Bonus: name a variant (SGD, Adam)

questions.question: How do you deploy a machine learning model to production?
points: Mention exporting/serializing the trained model
Wrapping it behind an API (e.g. Flask/FastAPI endpoint)
Mention monitoring for model drift after deployment
Bonus: containerization (Docker) for consistent environments

questions.question: What is a confusion matrix and why is it useful?
points: A table showing true/false positives and negatives
Helps compute precision, recall, F1-score
More informative than accuracy alone, especially for imbalanced data
Give a quick example of reading one

questions.question: What is transfer learning?
points: Using a pre-trained model as a starting point for a new task
Why: saves training time/data compared to training from scratch
Example: fine-tuning a pre-trained image or language model
Mention freezing early layers vs fine-tuning all layers

questions.question: What is the Activity lifecycle in Android?
points: Name the key stages: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy
Explain when each is triggered
Mention why understanding this matters (resource management, saving state)
Bonus: mention onSaveInstanceState for config changes

questions.question: What is the difference between a Fragment and an Activity?
points: Activity: a single screen with its own lifecycle
Fragment: a reusable portion of UI hosted within an Activity
Fragments have their own lifecycle tied to the host Activity
Why fragments: reusability, flexible layouts (tablets vs phones)

questions.question: What is Jetpack Compose and how is it different from the old View system?
points: Declarative UI toolkit vs the old imperative XML-based View system
You describe what the UI should look like for a given state
Less boilerplate, easier state management with recomposition
Bonus: mention it's now Google's recommended approach

questions.question: How do you handle background tasks in Android?
points: Mention Coroutines/WorkManager as modern approaches
Explain why you shouldn't block the main/UI thread
WorkManager for guaranteed deferrable background work
Bonus: mention older approaches (AsyncTask) are now deprecated

questions.question: What is CI/CD and why is it important?
points: CI: automatically building/testing code on every change
CD: automatically deploying code that passes those checks
Benefits: faster releases, fewer manual errors, quicker feedback
Bonus: name a tool (GitHub Actions, Jenkins)

questions.question: What is the difference between Docker and a virtual machine?
points: Docker: containers share the host OS kernel, lightweight
VM: full OS per instance, heavier, more isolated
Docker starts faster and uses fewer resources
Mention use case: consistent environments across dev/prod

questions.question: What is Kubernetes used for?
points: Orchestrating and managing containerized applications at scale
Handles scaling, load balancing, self-healing (restarting failed containers)
Mention pods, deployments, services as key concepts
Why: managing many containers manually doesn't scale

questions.question: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
points: Managing infrastructure through config files instead of manual setup
Benefits: version control, repeatability, faster provisioning
Name a tool (Terraform, Ansible)
Bonus: mention idempotency of IaC scripts

questions.question: What is the difference between a vulnerability, a threat, and a risk?
points: Vulnerability: a weakness that could be exploited
Threat: a potential event that could exploit a vulnerability
Risk: the likelihood and impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability
Give a simple example connecting all three

questions.question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
points: Attacker inserts malicious SQL through unsanitized user input
Prevention: parameterized queries/prepared statements
Mention input validation and least-privilege database accounts
Bonus: mention ORMs often prevent this by default

questions.question: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
points: Symmetric: same key for encryption and decryption, faster
Asymmetric: public/private key pair, used for secure key exchange
Mention a real use case for each
Bonus: mention HTTPS uses both (asymmetric for handshake, symmetric after)

questions.question: What is a firewall and how does it work?
points: A system that monitors/filters incoming and outgoing network traffic
Based on predefined security rules
Mention it can be hardware or software based
Bonus: distinguish stateful vs stateless firewalls

questions.question: What is the difference between UX and UI design?
points: UX: overall experience, usability, how it feels to use
UI: visual elements — colors, typography, layout
UX is broader and includes research; UI is more visual execution
Mention they work closely together, not interchangeable

questions.question: What is a user persona and why do designers create them?
points: A fictional representation of a target user based on research
Helps the team stay focused on real user needs, not assumptions
Usually includes goals, frustrations, behaviors
Bonus: mention it should be based on real user research, not guesses

questions.question: What is usability testing?
points: Observing real users interacting with a design to find pain points
Helps validate design decisions before/after development
Mention it can be done with low-fidelity prototypes too
Bonus: mention qualitative vs quantitative usability metrics

questions.question: What is the importance of accessibility in design?
points: Ensures the product is usable by people with disabilities
Mention color contrast, screen reader support, keyboard navigation
Reference WCAG guidelines if known
Why it matters: legal requirements + wider usable audience
